Four more Hamas operatives, including a terrorist who took part in the October 7 onslaught, were killed in recent strikes in the Gaza Strip, the military announces.
The IDF says that separate strikes on Saturday in northern Gaza killed Nabil Hamad, the head of a department in Hamas's "recruitment apparatus," and Mohannad Nader Mahmoud Dahdouh, a sniper commander.
Two other strikes in northern Gaza on October 22 killed Wael Naif Fahmi Muslim, a member of Hamas's elite Nukhba Force who invaded Israel on October 7, 2023, and Arafat Kamal Muhammad Ar'air, a rocket squad commander, the IDF says.
The IDF says all of the operatives had recently been advancing attacks on troops and Israeli civilians and acted to restore Hamas's capabilities, "in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

events.text:
🇨🇳 Chinese study finds premature damage in GE engines on Boeing 787s
Some high-pressure turbine blades in GE Aerospace's GEnx-1B engines developed cracks and shed pieces of material after relatively few flight cycles, according to a study cited by the South China Morning Post.
🔶 The damage can reportedly emerge within around 1,000 take-offs and landings, with cracks potentially spreading until fragments break away.
Xia Xiaofeng of Xiamen Airlines documented five engine removals in one 787 fleet caused by Phase 2/2+ blade defects — with GE attributing the cause to thermal fatigue. Some 417 GEnx engines worldwide, 15% of the global fleet, were still operating with the affected blades as of August 2025.
The findings add to scrutiny of Boeing 787 maintenance and US aerospace manufacturing quality following the 737 Max crashes, the Alaska Airlines door plug blowout, and the Air India 787 crash.
The study identifies thermal fatigue as the cause of the blade damage, while stressing the need for continued inspections and monitoring.

🗣“We’re starting from basically zero,” said Travis Metz, acting director of the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit. “None of them [manufacturing companies] have any scale in the US.”
The US Department of Defense is currently buying drones by the thousands, while competitors such as Russia and China are able to churn out millions of UAVs. The US is struggling to catch up, navigate supply chain challenges, and adapt to changing battlefield demands, Bloomberg reports.
👉 The Pentagon has committed about $1.1 billion to its Drone Dominance program, a four-stage competition that uses increasingly tougher tests and larger orders to determine which companies can manufacture drones at scale. Scrambling to close the gap, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth launched the Drone Dominance program in July last year in the latest effort to rapidly expand the American drone manufacturing base.
